planting.note: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, or again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Orazio matures quickly enough to fit both windows.

directions: Orazio is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid Florence fennel bred for uniform, thick, rounded bulbs that size up notably sooner than older open-pollinated strains. Direct sow into rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings early, since fennel's taproot makes it a poor candidate for transplanting. Harvest tender baby bulbs at around 50 days or let plants continue to full size; mounding soil around the swelling base as it develops helps keep the bulb pale and sweet rather than fibrous.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or succession-sow through summer for a fall crop, since Solaris is bred to bulb quickly across multiple seasonal slots.

directions: Solaris is an early F1 Florence fennel selected for stout, heavy bulbs that size up faster than most other bulbing types, making it a dependable choice for growers wanting an early harvest window. Sow directly into evenly moist, fertile soil and avoid root disturbance, since fennel seedlings transplant poorly once the taproot is established. The bulbs stay juicy and crisp rather than woody even as they reach 3 to 4 inches across, and the plant's dense feathery top can be harvested separately as a mild anise-flavored herb. Mound soil around the base as bulbs swell to keep them blanched and tender.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable, or sow again in midsummer for a fall-maturing crop, since Fino tends to bolt if grown through long, hot summer days.

directions: Fino is a traditional open-pollinated Florence fennel grown for its rounded, tightly layered white bulbs and sweet anise flavor. Direct sow into rich, evenly moist soil, since the taproot does not tolerate transplanting well, and thin seedlings to give bulbs room to expand. Being open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, Fino shows a bit more variability in bulb size and bolting tendency than modern F1 types, so timing sowings for cool conditions in spring or fall gives the most reliable results. Harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball to a fist, before any sign of a flowering stalk.
